p.src: Now the fifty defeated and surviving lesser demons, carrying tattered flags and broken drums, stumbled into the cave and reported, “Your Majesty, Tiger Vanguard could not overcome that hairy-faced monk and has been chased down the eastern slope.” On hearing this, the old demon was deeply troubled. As he sat with lowered head, saying nothing and silently devising a plan, another lesser demon guarding the front gate came to report, “Your Majesty, Tiger Vanguard has been slain by that hairy-faced monk, who has dragged his body to the gate and is hurling challenges at us.” At these words the old demon grew still more vexed and said, “That wretch truly has no sense. I never even ate his master, yet he has gone and killed my vanguard. Abominable! Abominable!” He cried, “Bring me my armor. I have only heard people speak of some Sun the Novice. Let me go out and see what sort of nine-headed, eight-tailed monk he is, seize him, and make him pay with his life for my Tiger Vanguard.” The lesser demons hurriedly carried out his armor. The old demon armed himself fully, snatched up a three-pronged steel fork, and led his demon horde leaping out of the cave.

p.src: The old demon came through the gate and shouted fiercely, “Which one of you is Sun the Novice?” With the tiger demon’s hide beneath his feet and the compliant iron staff in his hand, the Novice replied, “Your Grandpa Sun is here. Hand over my master.” The monster looked closely and saw that the Novice was puny in body, lean of face, and not even four feet tall. He laughed and said, “Pitiful, pitiful! I thought the mighty hero who overthrew my invincible vanguard would be something remarkable, but you are only a skeletal, sickly wretch.” The Novice laughed. “Son, you have no eye for things at all. Your grandpa may be small, but if you strike him on the head with the shaft of your fork, he will grow three feet taller.” The monster said, “Then brace your head and take a stroke from me.” The Great Sage showed not the slightest fear. The monster duly struck down at him. He merely bowed his waist, and at once grew three feet, until he stood some ten feet tall. Startled, the demon checked his steel fork and shouted, “Sun the Novice, why bring out such body-protecting transformations before my very gate? Enough of these empty tricks. Come forward and let us test each other’s skill.” The Novice laughed. “My son, as the saying goes, ‘If mercy stays your hand, do not raise it; once you raise it, show no mercy.’ Your grandpa’s hand is terribly heavy. I fear you could not withstand a single blow from this staff.” The monster would hear no more. Twirling his steel fork, he thrust it straight at the Novice’s chest; but the Great Sage was a true master who never flustered, unlike the flustered novice who has no mastery. He swung out his iron staff in the stance called “Black Dragon Skims the Earth,” knocked the steel fork aside, and struck at the monster’s head. There at the entrance to Yellow Wind Cave, the two fought a splendid battle:

p.src: The old demon and the Great Sage fought for thirty rounds without either gaining the upper hand. Eager to achieve a victory, the Novice employed his art of “bodies beyond the body”: he plucked out a handful of hairs, chewed them to pieces, sprayed them into the air, and cried, “Change!” They changed into more than a hundred Novices, all identically arrayed and each wielding an iron staff, surrounding the monster in midair. The monster took fright and used a special skill of his own. Turning quickly toward the southeast, he opened his mouth three times, then blew out a great breath with a whoosh. In an instant, a blast of yellow wind rose through the air. What a wind it was—fearsome indeed:

p.src: When the monster unleashed this furious gale, the little Novices transformed from the Great Sage Sun’s hairs were whirled about in midair like spinning wheels. How could they hope to swing their staffs or draw their bodies together? In alarm, the Novice shook his hairs and gathered them back onto his body. Then, alone, he raised his iron staff and advanced to attack. But the monster blew another mouthful of yellow wind directly into his face, forcing his fiery, golden-gazed eyes tightly shut so that he could not open them. Unable to wield his iron staff properly, he was forced to retreat from the fight. The demon then recalled the wind and returned to his cave; of him we speak no more for now.

p.src: Now Zhu Bajie, seeing the yellow wind rage until heaven and earth were dark, held the horse, guarded the luggage, and crouched in a hollow of the mountain. He dared neither open his eyes nor raise his head, but ceaselessly invoked the Buddha and made vows; nor did he know whether the Novice had won or lost, or whether his master was dead or alive. While he was anxiously wondering, the wind suddenly ceased and the sky cleared. He abruptly raised his head and looked toward the cave entrance, but saw no weapons and heard neither gong nor drum. The fool dared not approach their gate, yet there was no one to watch the horse and luggage. Truly caught between advance and retreat, he remained in a miserable panic. As he fretted, he heard the Great Sage Sun approaching from the west with a shout. Only then did he straighten up to meet him and say, “Brother, what a tremendous wind! Where have you come from?” The Novice waved his hand. “Fearsome, fearsome! In all my life, Old Sun has never encountered such a mighty wind. That old demon wielded a three-pronged steel fork and came out to fight Old Sun. After we had fought more than thirty rounds, Old Sun used the art of ‘bodies beyond the body.’ I surrounded him and attacked, and in his desperation he conjured up that gale. It was ferocious indeed. It blew so hard that I could not keep my feet, so I withdrew my magic and fled headlong through the wind. Hmph, what a wind! Hmph, what a wind! Old Sun can summon wind and call down rain, but I have never known a wind as vicious as that demon’s.” Bajie asked, “Elder Brother, how good is that demon at arms?” The Novice replied, “Respectable enough. His fork technique is quite polished, and he fought Old Sun to a draw. It is only that his wind is so vicious; defeating him will be difficult.” Bajie said, “If that is so, how can we rescue Master?” The Novice said, “We shall find another way to rescue Master presently. I wonder whether there is an eye doctor hereabouts. First let him treat my eyes.” Bajie asked, “What happened to your eyes?” The Novice replied, “The monster blew a mouthful of wind at me. It made my eyeballs ache and sting, and now cold tears keep streaming from them.” Bajie said, “Brother, we are halfway up a mountain and night is falling. Never mind finding an eye doctor—we do not even have a place to sleep.” The Novice said, “Finding lodging is not difficult. I reckon the demon still dares not harm our master. Let us return to the main road, find a household where we may stay the night, and come back to subdue the demon tomorrow at daybreak.” Bajie said, “Yes, indeed. That is best.”

p.src: They led the horse, shouldered the luggage, left the mountain hollow, and made their way to the road. By then dusk was gradually falling, and they heard dogs barking beneath a hillside south of the road. The two halted and looked. There stood a country estate, with the faint glow of lamps visible within. Whether there was a path or not, the two pushed through the wild grass and went straight to its gate. There they saw:

The two halted and looked. There stood a country estate, with the faint glow of lamps visible within.
Whether there was a path or not, the two pushed through the wild grass and went straight to its gate.
There they saw:

p.src: The two of them dared not enter unbidden, so they could only call out, “Open the gate! Open the gate!” An old man inside came over with several young farmhands, all bearing pitchforks, rakes, and brooms, and demanded, “Who is there? Who is there?” Pilgrim bowed and said, “We are disciples of a holy monk from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land. On our journey west to worship the Buddha and obtain the scriptures, we passed this mountain, where the Great King Yellow Wind seized our master, whom we have not yet managed to rescue. As night has fallen, we have come expressly to ask for lodging at your house for one night. We earnestly beg your kindness.” The old man returned his salute and said, “Forgive us for failing to welcome you properly. This is a place of many clouds and few people. When we heard someone calling at the gate just now, we feared it might be fox demons, tigers, mountain bandits, or the like. That is why these ignorant young servants behaved so rudely; we did not know that you were two reverend monks. Please come in, please come in.”

p.src: The two brothers led the horse and carried the luggage inside. They went straight into the house, tethered the horse, set down the load, and exchanged greetings with the old master of the farmstead before taking their seats. An old servant brought them tea. When they had finished the tea, several bowls of sesame rice were served. After the meal, the old man ordered bedding laid out for them to sleep. Pilgrim said, “I can manage without sleep, but may I ask, good sir, whether anyone hereabouts sells eye medicine?” The old man asked, “Which of you reverend monks has trouble with his eyes?” Pilgrim replied, “To tell you the truth, venerable sir, we men of religion have always been free from illness and know nothing of eye ailments.” The old man said, “If your eyes are not afflicted, why ask for medicine?” Pilgrim said, “Today, while we were trying to rescue our master at the entrance to Yellow Wind Cave, that monster unexpectedly blew a gust of wind at me. It made my eyeballs smart and ache, and now they are brimming with tears. That is why I seek eye medicine.” The old man exclaimed, “Mercy, mercy! Reverend sir, young as you are, how can you tell such lies? The Great King Yellow Wind's wind is most fearsome. It is nothing like the winds of spring and autumn, the wind through pines and bamboo, or winds from east, west, south, and north. …” Bajie said, “Could it be a wind that grips the brain, a sheep-ear wind, leprous wind, or a one-sided or full headache wind?” The elder said, “No, no. It is called the Divine Wind of Samadhi.” Pilgrim asked, “How can that be seen?” The old man replied, “That wind can blow heaven and earth into darkness and sweep sorrow through ghosts and gods; viciously it splits rocks and shatters cliffs, and when it strikes a man, his life is ended. If that wind truly struck you, could you still hope to live? Only an immortal could escape unharmed.” Pilgrim said, “True enough, true enough. Though we are not immortals, immortals are still my juniors. My life will not be ended so readily; the wind merely made my eyeballs smart and ache.” The old man said, “If that is so, you must indeed be someone of extraordinary origins. There is no one in this humble place of ours who sells eye medicine. But this old man also suffers somewhat from tears brought on by cold winds. I once met an extraordinary person who taught me a remedy called Three-Flower Nine-Seed Ointment, which can cure every wind-borne affliction of the eyes.” Hearing this, Pilgrim bowed his head and saluted, saying, “I beg you for a little, that I may try applying it.” The old man agreed and immediately went inside. He returned with a little agate jar, removed its stopper, dipped out a small amount with a jade hairpin, and applied it to Pilgrim's eyes. He told him not to open them, but to calm his mind and sleep, and they would be well by morning. After applying the medicine, he put away the stone jar and led the young servants straight back inside.

p.src: Bajie untied the bundle, spread out the bedding, and invited Pilgrim to lie down. Pilgrim groped about blindly with his eyes closed. Bajie laughed and said, “Sir, where is your blind man's staff?” Pilgrim replied, “You meal-swilling idiot! Do you take me for a blind man?” The idiot chuckled secretly to himself and went to sleep. Pilgrim sat upon the bedding and circulated his divine power, not lying down to sleep until after the third watch.

p.src: Before they knew it, the fifth watch had come and dawn was near. Pilgrim rubbed his face, opened his eyes, and said, “It truly is good medicine! My sight is a hundredfold brighter than usual.” But when he turned his head and looked behind him—ah! There were no houses, windows, or doors to be seen. There were only old locust trees and tall willows, and the two brothers had been sleeping upon a carpet of green grass. Bajie awoke and asked, “Brother, what are you shouting about?” Pilgrim said, “Open your eyes and look.” The idiot suddenly raised his head and, seeing the household gone, scrambled anxiously to his feet and cried, “Where is my horse?” Pilgrim said, “Is that not it, tethered to the tree?” “And the luggage?” Pilgrim said, “Is that not it beside your head?” Bajie said, “What a lazy family! If they were moving away, why did they not call out to us? Had old Hog known, we could at least have given them some tea and fruit for the road. They must have been evading their household obligations and feared the village chief would learn of it, so they moved away during the night. —Good heavens! We must have slept far too soundly. How could they dismantle the house without our hearing so much as a single crash?” Pilgrim chuckled and said, “Idiot, stop shouting nonsense. Look—what is that paper notice on the tree?” Bajie went forward and peeled it off with his hand. Written upon it were these four lines of verse:

p.src: Pilgrim said, “These overbearing gods! Ever since we exchanged the dragon for the horse, I have not once called the roll on them, and now they have come to play tricks again.” Bajie said, “Brother, do not put on airs. Why should they submit to your inspection and command?” Pilgrim replied, “Brother, there is something you still do not know. These Guardian Garans of the Faith, the Six Ding and Six Jia, the Guardians of the Five Directions, and the Duty Officers of the Four Watches obey the Bodhisattva's decree and secretly protect our master. Since the day they reported their names, I have had you with me and have had no occasion to employ them, so I simply have not called their roll.” Bajie said, “Brother, since they obey a decree to protect Master in secret, they cannot openly show themselves. That is why they conjured up an immortal farmstead. Do not blame them. Yesterday you had them to thank for treating your eyes, and they also provided us with a vegetarian meal. They may surely be said to have done their utmost. Do not blame them; let us go and rescue Master.” Pilgrim said, “Brother, you are right. The entrance to Yellow Wind Cave is not far from here. Do not set out yet; stay in the woods to watch the horse and guard the luggage. Let old Sun go into the cave to investigate and learn what has become of Master; then I will do battle with the monster.” Bajie said, “That is just what we should do—obtain definite news whether he is dead or alive. If Master is dead, each of us can seek his own way and occupation; but if he is not, we can devote all our strength and effort to saving him.” Pilgrim said, “Do not talk nonsense. I am off.”

p.src: With one bound he went straight to the cave entrance, where the gate was still shut and its keepers asleep. Pilgrim did not call at the gate, for he wished not to alarm the monsters. Instead, he made the hand sign, recited a spell, shook himself, and transformed into a spotted-legged mosquito, truly tiny and nimble. A poem bears witness to this. The poem says:

Pilgrim did not call at the gate, for he wished not to alarm the monsters. Instead, he made the hand sign, recited a spell, shook himself, and transformed into a spotted-legged mosquito, truly tiny and nimble.

The poem says:

p.src: He saw the little monster guarding the gate snoring in his sleep. Pilgrim bit him on the face, and the little monster rolled over and awoke, crying, “Oh, my lord! What a huge mosquito! One bite has raised a great lump.” Suddenly opening his eyes wide, he said, “It is daylight.” Then came a creak, and the inner gate opened. Pilgrim flew inside with a faint buzz. There he saw the old monster ordering strict vigilance at every gate while having the weapons made ready: “I fear yesterday's wind may not have blown Sun the Pilgrim to death. He is certain to return today, and when he comes, I shall make sure his life is ended.”

Then came a creak, and the inner gate opened.

Pilgrim flew inside with a faint buzz. p.src: Hearing this, the Pilgrim flew back across the hall and went straight to the rear, where he found a tightly shut gate. He slipped through a crack in the gate and found himself in a large empty garden. Over to one side, the Tang Monk was bound hand and foot with ropes to a wind-stilling post. Tears streamed from the master's eyes as his thoughts dwelt only on Wukong and Wuneng, for he knew not where either of them was. The Pilgrim stilled his wings, alighted on the master's bald head, and called, “Master.” Recognizing his voice, the elder said, “Wukong! How desperately I have longed for you. Where are you calling me from?” The Pilgrim replied, “Master, I am on top of your head. Do not be anxious or distressed. We must capture the fiend before we can save your life.” The Tang Monk asked, “Disciple, when will you be able to catch the fiend?” The Pilgrim said, “The tiger fiend who seized you has already been beaten to death by Bajie. Only the old fiend's wind is formidable. I reckon that today, without fail, we shall capture him. Set your mind at ease and do not cry. I am going now.”

Had I not run quickly, he would nearly have caught me. p.src: From the roof beam, the Pilgrim heard these words and was overjoyed. He immediately flew out, resumed his true form, went to the woods, and called, “Brother!” Bajie said, “Brother, where have you been? Just now I chased away a fiend carrying a command pennant.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Well done, well done! I changed myself into a mosquito and entered his cave to look for Master. It turns out they have tied him to a wind-stilling post, where he sits weeping. I told him not to cry. Then I flew up to the roof beam and listened. The pennant-bearing fellow came rushing in, panting, to report that you had chased him; but he had not seen me. The old fiend made all manner of wild guesses, saying either that the wind had killed me or that I had gone to summon divine troops. But then he himself let slip the name of a certain person. Excellent, excellent!” Bajie asked, “Whom did he name?” The Pilgrim replied, “He said that he feared no divine troops, and that only the Bodhisattva Lingji could subdue the force of his wind. But I do not know where Lingji lives.”

p.src: Bajie was delighted to see him and said, “Elder Brother, as the saying goes, ‘To learn the road below the mountain, ask one who has traveled it.’ Why not go and ask him?” The Great Sage duly concealed his iron staff, let down the front of his robe, went forward, and called, “Greetings, venerable sir.” The old man barely returned his greeting and asked, “Where are you monks from? What business brings you to this wilderness?” The Pilgrim replied, “We are holy monks journeying to fetch the scriptures. Yesterday our master was lost here, so we have come especially to ask you where the Bodhisattva Lingji lives.” The old man said, “Lingji is due south of here, three thousand li away. There is a mountain called Little Sumeru, and within it stands a monastery where the Bodhisattva expounds the scriptures. Are you going to fetch his scriptures?” The Pilgrim said, “We are not going to fetch his scriptures. I have a matter in which I require his help, but do not know which road to take.” Pointing south with his hand, the old man said, “That narrow, winding path is the one.” He tricked the Great Sage Sun into turning his head to look at the road; then the old man transformed into a clear breeze and silently vanished. Only a note remained beside the road, bearing a verse of four lines:

p.src: The Pilgrim took up the note, turned around, and came back down the road. Bajie said, “Brother, our luck has been poor these past few days. For two days running, we have seen ghosts in broad daylight. Who was that old fellow who turned into wind?” The Pilgrim handed the note to Bajie, who read it through and asked, “Who is Li Changgeng?” The Pilgrim replied, “It is the name of the Great White Planet of the West.” Alarmed, Bajie bowed toward the sky and cried, “My benefactor, my benefactor! Had the Gold Star not petitioned the Jade Emperor on my behalf, who knows what would have become of old Hog's life?” The Pilgrim said, “Brother, so you do know gratitude. But do not show yourself. Hide deep in these woods and guard the baggage and horse carefully. Wait here while I seek Mount Sumeru and invite the Bodhisattva.” Bajie said, “I understand, I understand. Just hurry on your way. Old Hog has learned the tortoise's art: when it is time to draw in my head, I shall draw it in.”

p.src: The Great Sage Sun leapt into the air, mounted his somersault cloud, and sped due south. Swift indeed was he: a nod of his head carried him three thousand li, and a twist of his waist more than eight hundred leagues. Presently he saw a lofty mountain, halfway up which auspicious clouds appeared and blessed vapors billowed. In a hollow of the mountain there was indeed a monastery. The melodious ringing of bells and chimes could be heard, while fragrant smoke drifted through the air. The Great Sage went straight to the gate, where he saw a religious attendant with prayer beads around his neck, reciting the Buddha's name. The Pilgrim said, “Greetings, good sir.” The attendant bowed in return and asked, “Where have you come from, honored sir?” The Pilgrim asked, “Is this where the Bodhisattva Lingji expounds the scriptures?” The attendant replied, “It is indeed. What business have you?” The Pilgrim said, “Please trouble yourself to announce me. I am Sun Wukong the Pilgrim, the Great Sage Equaling Heaven, disciple of the imperial younger brother of His Majesty of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, the Dharma Master Tripitaka. I have business today and wish to see the Bodhisattva.” The attendant laughed. “Honored sir, you have too many titles and too many words. I cannot remember them all.” The Pilgrim said, “Just say that Sun Wukong, disciple of the Tang Monk, has come.”

p.src: The Bodhisattva straightened his robes and came out to welcome him. The Pilgrim entered the hall and took the guest seat, whereupon tea was ordered. The Pilgrim said, “Please do not trouble yourself with tea. My master is in peril at Yellow Wind Mountain, and I have come especially to ask the Bodhisattva to exert your great powers, subdue the monster, and save him.” The Bodhisattva said, “I received the Tathagata’s command to keep the Yellow Wind Monster suppressed here. The Tathagata gave me a Wind-Stilling Pearl and a Flying Dragon Staff. When I captured him before, I spared his life and released him to conceal his powers and return to the mountains, forbidding him to kill living creatures or commit further evil. I did not know that today he meant to harm your honored master. Since he has disobeyed my injunction, the fault is mine.” The Bodhisattva wished to keep the Pilgrim there and prepare a vegetarian meal while they conversed, but the Pilgrim earnestly declined. The Bodhisattva then took up the Flying Dragon Staff and mounted the clouds together with the Great Sage.

p.src: Before long, they arrived above Yellow Wind Mountain. The Bodhisattva said, “Great Sage, this monster is somewhat afraid of me. I shall remain hidden among the clouds while you go down and challenge him. Lure him outside, and I shall employ my powers.” The Pilgrim obeyed, lowered his cloud, and without another word drew his iron staff and smashed open the cave gate. He cried, “Monster! Give me back my master!” The little fiends guarding the gate were so alarmed that they hurried inside to report it. The monster said, “That insolent monkey is truly outrageous! Not only does he still refuse to submit, but he has even smashed my gate. This time I shall go out, raise a divine gale, and blow him to his death without fail.” He armed himself as before, grasped his steel trident, and once more strode out through the gate. On seeing the Pilgrim, he spoke not a word but twirled his trident and thrust it straight at his chest; the Great Sage turned sideways and dodged the blow. He raised his staff and struck back. After only a few exchanges, the monster wheeled around toward the southeast and was just opening his mouth to summon the wind when Lingji Bodhisattva, high in the air, hurled down the Flying Dragon Staff. No one knew what spell he recited, but the staff became an eight-clawed golden dragon. With a sudden sweep it spread two claws, seized the fiend in one grip, lifted him by the head, and dashed him two or three times against the rocky cliff. The monster then revealed his true form: a yellow-furred marten.

p.src: The Pilgrim rushed forward and raised his staff to strike, but the Bodhisattva stopped him, saying, “Great Sage, do not take his life. I must still bring him before the Tathagata.” He then said to the Pilgrim, “He was originally a rat that attained the Way at the foot of Spirit Mountain. Because he stole the pure oil from a crystal lamp, causing its flame to dim, he feared the Vajra guardians would seize him and therefore fled. He later became a monster here and began making trouble. The Tathagata perceived what had happened and judged that his offense did not warrant death, so he ordered me to keep him under restraint. But he has killed living creatures and accumulated evil deeds, and must now be taken up to Spirit Mountain. Now he has also offended the Great Sage and plotted against the Tang Monk. I shall take him before the Tathagata so that his crimes may be formally judged; only then will this deed be complete.” On hearing this, the Pilgrim thanked the Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva returned westward, and of that we shall say no more.

p.src: Now Zhu Bajie, waiting in the woods and thinking anxiously of the Pilgrim, suddenly heard a voice call from below the hillside, “Brother Wuneng, bring the horse and luggage!” The fool recognized the Pilgrim’s voice, hurriedly gathered everything up, and ran out of the woods. When he saw the Pilgrim, he said, “Brother, how did things go?” The Pilgrim said, “I invited Lingji Bodhisattva here, and he used the Flying Dragon Staff to capture the fiend. It turned out to be a yellow-furred marten that had become a monster. The Bodhisattva has taken it to Spirit Mountain to appear before the Tathagata. You and I will go into the cave and rescue Master.” Only then did the fool become thoroughly delighted.

p.src: The two burst inside and, with rake and iron staff, mercilessly killed the entire den of cunning hares, demon foxes, musk deer, and antlered deer. They then went to the rear garden, paid their respects, and rescued their master. When the master came out through the gate, he asked, “How did you two capture the fiend? And how were you finally able to rescue me?” The Pilgrim recounted the whole affair of inviting Lingji Bodhisattva to subdue the monster. The master could not thank them enough. The disciples prepared some vegetarian provisions from the cave and ate a meal with tea. Only then did they leave, find the main road, and continue westward.
